statement: The central idea of cloud computing is buying compute rather than buying a computer — trading capital expenditure on physical hardware for operational expenditure on rented compute time owned by a third party.

Infrastructure as a Service (IaaS) lets organizations outsource not just hardware but also the undifferentiated software layers — operating systems, databases, clustering, networking, monitoring, high availability — reducing the gap between application code and raw compute.

Before DevOps, development and operations were two separate organizational functions with different incentives — developers focused on shipping new features quickly while operations teams prioritized long-term stability — which frequently created conflict.

The DevOps movement originated as an effort to bring development and operations together to collaborate, share responsibility for system reliability and software correctness, and improve the feedback loops between code authoring, testing, and deployment.
DevOps is primarily an organizational and human issue, not a technical one — the most critical changes are cultural and collaborative rather than tooling choices.

The NoOps view — that cloud and containers eliminate the need for operations staff — is a fallacy; in DevOps, monitoring, logging, A/B testing, CI/CD pipelines, and policy checks happen before production rather than during post-outage firefighting.

Infrastructure as Code means cloud infrastructure is automatically provisioned by software rather than by manual physical racking and cabling, turning operations engineering into a software discipline.

The software container concept parallels the shipping container: a standard, generic packaging format that carries all dependencies, enabling economies of scale, lower costs, and greatly simplified handling.

Container images are substantially smaller than virtual machine images — a typical VM image is around 1 GiB while a well-designed container image may be a hundred times smaller — because containers do not bundle unrelated programs and use shared addressable filesystem layers.
Containers run directly on the real CPU with no virtualization overhead, whereas virtualized workloads run approximately 30% slower than equivalent containers due to the emulated CPU layer.

The container is simultaneously the unit of deployment, packaging, reuse, scaling, and resource allocation — a single container image can serve as a component of many different services and can run wherever sufficient resources are available.
A container orchestrator joins many different machines into a unified compute cluster that appears to users as a single powerful computer, handling scheduling, orchestration, and cluster management.

Kubernetes was founded as an open-source project by Google in 2014, derived from lessons learned in their internal Borg and Omega systems, and has become the de facto standard for container orchestration — adoption more than doubling since 2017 with half of container-running organizations using it.
Kubernetes automates traditional sysadmin tasks — server upgrades, security patching, network configuration, load balancing, autoscaling — so that teams can concentrate on their core work.
Kubernetes enables zero-downtime deployments by default through rolling updates — starting containers with the new version, waiting until they become healthy, then shutting down the old ones.

Kubernetes supports canary deployments — gradually rolling out updates one server at a time to catch problems early — and blue-green deployments — spinning up a new version in parallel and switching traffic once fully running.
Kubernetes autoscaling can add new Pod replicas when CPU utilization exceeds a threshold, and scale down when demand falls, freeing cluster capacity for other workloads.

Kubernetes is provider-agnostic: applications defined using Kubernetes resources can run on any Kubernetes cluster regardless of underlying cloud provider, with Kubernetes mapping resources to vendor-specific features such as load balancers.

Running stateful workloads such as databases in Kubernetes requires careful engineering for restarts, data consistency, and schema coordination across replicas — database replicas are not interchangeable and each has a unique state.

For stateful workloads like databases, using a managed database service is usually more cost-effective than running them in Kubernetes, due to the large engineering investment required for enterprise-grade reliability.
exception: If the organization has a dedicated team with Kubernetes stateful-workload expertise

statement: FaaS platforms such as AWS Lambda are best suited to short, standalone, event-driven jobs (Lambda limits functions to 15 minutes) that integrate with cloud services, rather than long-running application servers.
exception: Long-running workloads are better suited to containers or managed Kubernetes

statement: Cloud-native applications must be automatable — they must abide by common standards, formats, and interfaces so that they can be deployed and managed by machines rather than humans.

Containerized microservices are ubiquitous and flexible because they are decoupled from physical resources and specific knowledge of the compute node, making them easy to move between nodes or clusters.

Traditional applications have single points of failure at the process, hardware, or network level; cloud-native applications achieve high availability through inherent distribution, redundancy, and graceful degradation.

Observability — monitoring, logging, tracing, and metrics — is a key requirement of cloud-native distributed systems because they are inherently harder to inspect and debug than monolithic applications.
Cloud-native applications are composed of multiple cooperating distributed microservices rather than deployed as a single monolith — a microservice is a self-contained service that does one thing.

Microservices are not a panacea: monoliths are easier to understand and trace, but hard to scale; even a well-designed microservices architecture is a distributed system that is inherently complex, difficult to observe, and prone to surprising failures.

Running monolithic applications in the cloud using containers is still feasible and can deliver significant business value — it may serve as a transitional step toward gradually extracting microservices.

In cloud-native organizations, operations expertise is distributed across development teams rather than concentrated in a single central ops team — each team needs an operations specialist responsible for system health, networking, and resilience.

At approximately 75 engineers, organizations naturally develop a central infrastructure team; beyond a certain scale this team can no longer build infrastructure and maintain the support burden simultaneously, motivating embedded site reliability engineers in product teams.

Using multi-stage Docker builds (a build stage plus a scratch final stage) produces minimal container images: a Go binary ends up around 6 MiB versus roughly 350 MiB without the second stage, giving a 98% size reduction.
Minimal container images improve deployment speed (faster upload/download/startup) and reduce security attack surface because fewer programs mean fewer potential vulnerabilities.

Processes in a container are isolated from the host and cannot access network ports directly; to expose a container port, a host port must be explicitly forwarded to the container port using the -p HOST_PORT:CONTAINER_PORT flag.

A container registry stores and retrieves container images using a unique name or URL; the default registry for Docker is Docker Hub, but organizations can specify alternatives or self-host their own registry.

The Kubernetes control plane consists of five components: kube-apiserver (API frontend), etcd (cluster state database), kube-scheduler (Pod placement), kube-controller-manager (resource controllers), and cloud-controller-manager (cloud provider integration).

Each Kubernetes worker node runs three components: kubelet (drives the container runtime and monitors workload status), kube-proxy (handles inter-Pod and Pod-to-internet networking), and a container runtime (starts/stops containers — historically Docker, now commonly containerd or CRI-O).
The etcd database is replicated across multiple nodes and can survive the failure of individual nodes as long as a quorum of more than half the original etcd replicas remains available.

High availability of the Kubernetes control plane is critical: control plane failure stops new deployments and breaks controllers even if existing Pods keep running; production clusters need a minimum of three control plane nodes to maintain quorum when one fails.

Failure of a single worker node should not affect applications configured to run with more than one replica; Kubernetes detects the failure and reschedules the node's Pods elsewhere as long as the control plane is operational.
condition: Applications have more than one replica

statement: Worker nodes should be distributed across multiple cloud availability zones rather than concentrated in one zone, because losing an entire availability zone is a rare but entirely possible event.

HA configuration should be actively tested — not just assumed — by deliberately rebooting worker nodes and control plane nodes during a maintenance window to verify that the cluster survives and that kubectl remains functional.

A self-hosted Kubernetes cluster ready for production must address at least eight areas beyond basic setup: control-plane HA, worker-node HA, cluster security (TLS, RBAC, etcd access control), service security, conformance, configuration management of nodes, data backup and restore, and ongoing maintenance procedures.

Self-hosting Kubernetes is not just an initial setup cost — it requires continuous monitoring, alerting, keeping up with new Kubernetes releases, regular resilience testing (e.g., using Chaos Monkey), and reprovisioning to take advantage of new features.

The majority of Kubernetes setup tools solve only easy problems while ignoring the hard ones; powerful enterprise-grade tools tend to be very expensive or unavailable to the public, as vendors prefer to sell managed services.

Kubernetes is hard: despite being well-designed for its complexity, there is a significant investment of time and energy involved in both learning to manage clusters properly and doing so from day to day.

Using a managed Kubernetes service is recommended over self-hosting the control plane — it is far more cost-effective for almost all businesses, and there are basically no good reasons to self-host unless the requirements are unusual or unsupported by managed providers.
exception: Requirements that no managed provider supports

statement: A fully working, secure, highly available, production-grade Kubernetes cluster can be obtained from a managed service in a few minutes for a few dollars a day, with most cloud providers offering free tiers for weeks or months.

Managed Kubernetes services relieve organizations of almost all control-plane administration overhead — the provider handles scheduling, monitoring, failover, and security patching of the cluster's brain.

GKE supports multizone and regional clusters that spread worker nodes (and control plane nodes) across multiple failure zones, keeping workloads running even if an entire data center zone is affected by an outage.

GKE cluster autoscaling adds nodes when pending workloads are waiting for capacity and removes unused nodes when there is spare capacity, helping control costs because GKE billing is based on the number of worker nodes.

GKE Autopilot fully manages both control plane and worker nodes, billing only for the CPU and memory that Pods request rather than for underlying VMs — suitable for teams that want Kubernetes flexibility without managing server infrastructure.

Amazon EKS manages the control plane nodes; however, compared to other hosted offerings it provides a less 'batteries-included' experience — features such as centralized logging with CloudWatch and cluster autoscaling require additional configuration after cluster creation.

The 'Run Less Software' philosophy has three pillars: choose standard technology, outsource undifferentiated heavy lifting, and create enduring competitive advantage — applicable to Kubernetes cluster decisions.

Installing, configuring, maintaining, securing, upgrading, and making a Kubernetes cluster reliable is undifferentiated heavy lifting that does not differentiate a business; outsourcing it to a managed service is economically rational for almost all organizations.

Vendor lock-in from managed Kubernetes is less severe than commonly feared: Kubernetes abstracts cloud-specific details into a standard API, and as long as applications target Kubernetes manifests rather than cloud infrastructure directly, they remain portable across certified providers with minor tweaks.

Self-hosting Kubernetes actually increases cloud-vendor lock-in rather than reducing it, because provisioning the cluster's underlying compute requires completely different provider-specific code (e.g., AWS vs. Google Cloud).

Being cloud-native does not require a public cloud provider — organizations can run Kubernetes on bare-metal hardware (on-premises or co-located) and gain the same benefits of containers and orchestration.

Kubernetes serves as a standardization layer across multi-cloud and hybrid-cloud environments; tools such as VMware Tanzu Mission Control and Google Anthos allow central management of multiple clusters running across different cloud providers and on-premises.

Most small and mid-sized teams should not start with multi-cloud Kubernetes infrastructure — the additional complexity and cost are not justified at that scale; start with basics (containers on a single managed Kubernetes offering) and build up from there.

When self-hosting Kubernetes is unavoidable, the recommended tools are kops (for AWS and growing multi-cloud support) or Kubespray (for on-premises and any cloud, using Ansible), as both are mature and production-grade.

Clusterless container services (Amazon Fargate, Azure Container Instances, Google Cloud Run) eliminate cluster management entirely; the user specifies a container image and resource requirements and the provider runs it — ideal for simple long-running tasks, batch jobs, build containers, and burst workloads.

kops is a mature, widely used command-line tool for automated provisioning of high-availability Kubernetes clusters, originally AWS-specific but adding support for Google Cloud, DigitalOcean, Azure, and OpenStack; it uses declarative configuration and supports scaling, resizing, and upgrades.

Kubespray is focused on installing production-ready Kubernetes clusters on existing machines, including on-premise and bare-metal servers, using Ansible Playbooks, and is suitable for any cloud or private cloud environment.

OpenShift is a full Platform-as-a-Service product that extends Kubernetes with continuous integration, build tools, test runners, deployment, monitoring, and orchestration, deployable across bare-metal, VMs, private clouds, and public clouds — well-suited to very large organizations with heterogeneous infrastructure.

Docker comprises a container image format, a runtime library managing container lifecycle, a CLI for packaging and running containers, and an API for container management; a container image is a single binary file holding everything needed to run the container.

A Dockerfile specifies exactly what goes into a container image using instructions that start from a base image, transform it, and save the result — supporting multi-stage builds where intermediate build artifacts do not end up in the final production image.

ErrImagePull or ImagePullBackoff Pod status in Kubernetes indicates that the cluster could not find or download the specified container image — typically caused by a typo in the image name or missing registry credentials.
The kubectl tool is the primary interface for interacting with a Kubernetes cluster and can be used both imperatively (direct resource creation) and declaratively (applying YAML manifests).
